questions.q: What is the **minimum detectable effect** (MDE) in an A/B test?
options: The smallest p-value the test can produce
The lowest conversion rate seen in either group
The effect observed at the end of the test
The smallest improvement worth detecting, chosen in advance as a business decision; it drives the required sample size
questions.why: The MDE is set before the test: the smallest lift that would justify acting. Smaller MDEs need much larger samples (halving it roughly quadruples n). It is not the observed effect and has nothing to do with p-values.

questions.q: Which of these should be decided **before** an A/B test starts?
options: The primary metric, the MDE, α, power and therefore the sample size
Which metric looked best after the test
Whether to use a one-sided test, based on early results
When to stop, based on daily p-values
questions.why: Fixing these up front protects against p-hacking. Choosing the metric, the sidedness or the stopping point after seeing data inflates the false-positive rate.

questions.q: Control: 8,000 visitors, 400 purchases (5.0%). Variant: 8,000 visitors, 480 purchases (6.0%). Using a pooled two-proportion z-test, what are z and the two-sided p-value?
questions.why: Pooled rate = 880 / 16,000 = 5.5%. SE = √(0.055 × 0.945 × (1/8,000 + 1/8,000)) = 0.0036. z = 0.010 / 0.0036 = 2.77, two-sided p ≈ 0.0055. 0.003 is the one-sided tail; z = 1.00 forgets to divide by the SE (it is the lift in points).

questions.q: A test with 1,000 visitors per arm shows a lift of 1.5 points, p = 0.15, 95% CI −0.5 to +3.5 points. What is the right conclusion?
options: Variant B does not work; drop it
Inconclusive: the test was too small to tell, and the truth could be anywhere from slightly worse to much better
Variant B works; a 30% relative lift is huge
The confidence interval is wrong because it includes negative values
questions.why: Not significant with a wide interval means the test lacked power, not that B fails. About 3,800 visitors per arm were needed to detect this lift with 80% power. Claiming success ignores the fact that zero (and slight harm) is still plausible.

questions.q: A test was planned with about 10,300 visitors per arm to detect a lift from 4.0% to 4.8%. The team now wants to detect 4.0% to 4.4% instead (α = 5%, power = 80%). Roughly how many visitors per arm are needed?
options: About 5,150
About 20,600
About 10,300
About 39,500
questions.why: Required n scales with 1 / MDE². Halving the MDE from 0.8 to 0.4 points roughly quadruples n: 7.85 × (0.04 × 0.96 + 0.044 × 0.956) / 0.004² ≈ 39,500. Doubling (20,600) is the common intuition, and it leaves the test badly under-powered.

questions.q: A product manager checks the A/B dashboard daily and plans to stop the moment p drops below 0.05. Why is this a problem?
options: Repeated peeking gives many chances for random noise to cross 0.05, inflating the false-positive rate well above 5%; use a fixed sample size or a sequential method designed for monitoring
It is fine; stopping early saves traffic
Daily checks make the p-value too large
It only matters for one-sided tests
questions.why: Each look is another test. Stopping at the first crossing turns a 5% false-alarm rate into a much higher one. Sequential testing with adjusted thresholds, or a Bayesian analysis with a pre-agreed rule, allows monitoring safely.

questions.q: A planned test (10,500 per arm) gives 4.0% versus 4.8%, p = 0.005, 95% CI for the lift +0.25 to +1.35 points. Even the low end is worth about ₹15,000 a day. What is the soundest reason to ship B?
options: p = 0.005 means a 99.5% chance B is better
The observed lift is 20%, which is large
The whole interval is above zero, and even its cautious end is commercially worthwhile
B had more purchases, so it must be better
questions.why: The decision rests on the range of plausible effects: all positive, and even the smallest is worth the change. A p-value is not the probability that B is better, and a raw count or observed lift on its own ignores uncertainty.

questions.q: In an interview: "A 50/50 test ended with 10,300 users in A and 9,700 in B. Anything to worry about?"
options: No, a 300-user gap is small
Yes: a chi-square goodness-of-fit test against 10,000 each gives χ² = 18, p ≈ 0.00002, a sample-ratio mismatch; the assignment or logging is broken, so investigate before trusting any result
Only if the conversion rates differ
No, just analyse the data with weights
questions.why: χ² = (300² + 300²) / 10,000 = 18 with 1 degree of freedom, p ≈ 2 × 10⁻⁵, far too unlikely for a fair split. Sample-ratio mismatch usually means some users were lost or mis-assigned non-randomly (for example a bug in one variant), which can bias the comparison. Reweighting does not repair a broken randomisation.
